Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-12-29
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Ava Patel, Marco Li (Redwood); Priya Nair, Ethan Morales, Sara Kim (Beacon)
Recording id: ff-20251229-7a3b

Auto-summary (auto): quick architecture sanity for dedicated vs hosted: focus on tenant fencing, KV prefetch/pinning, batching strategies to hit 99th p50 targets, tradeoffs of quantization and VPC onprem network egress.
Topics: tenant fencing, kv prefetch, batching windows, int8 quantization, VPC peering, KMS/audit logs, pilot plan

Transcript:
00:00 Ava: ok great thanks everyone for joining, I think we have about an hour. quick intros?
00:07 Priya: hey this is Priya Nair, VP Eng at Beacon, iam focusing on inference infra and latency SLOs.
00:12 Ethan: Ethan here, infra lead, run our k8s and private cloud.
:14 Sara: Sara, ML engineer, owns model serving and prompt sets.
00:20 Ava: from Redwood I am Ava, AE. Marco is our performance SE.
00:25 Marco: hey all, thanks. i put a short runbook and a KV benchmark sheet in the chat, link: https://redwood.internal/benchmarks/kv-prefetch.xlsx (note: internal link - will share updated).
00:38 Priya: perfect, our main ask - we need to understand if Dedicated pools will give us predictable 99th latency under high concurrency, and what isolation mechanisms you recommend for noisy neighbors.
00:48 Marco: got it. quick context question, what is your current seq-length dist? average prompt ~120 tokens, but with some longer clinical notes up to 1,500 tokens. is that right?
00:59 Sara: yes p95 is about 900 tokens for our long diagnosis summaries. p99 spikes are the pain point.
01:05 Ethan: and our client side concurrency bursts during EMR syncs are kind of spiky - we see lots of parallel requests for batches.
01:12 Ava: ok so we need to cover two axes: isolation/fencing and request-level optimizations (kv prefetch, batching, quantization).
01:21 Priya: also security - we will likely need VPC or on-prem, KMS key control, SOC2 and audit trail.
01:27 Marco: totally, we design with that in mind. on the fencing topic, we have three practical patterns: physical dedicated pools (per-tenant GPU pools), soft fencing with tenant-aware scheduling, and hybrid fencing that pins hot KV cache to tenant-local memory.
01:43 Ethan: can you elaborate on "tenant-aware scheduling"? we are worried about noisy-tenants stealing tokens.
01:49 Marco: sure. tenant-aware scheduling is the runtime assigning isolation weights and dynamic windowing to maintain per-tenant latencies - it prioritizes small requests and can preempt large background jobs. it's lighter weight than full dedicated pools. caveat: it's multi-tenant so tail latency can still be impacted by extreme outliers.
02:05 Priya: and dedicated pools means reserved GPUs per tenant which is costly but more predictable?
02:10 Marco: exactly. dedicated gives near-linear isolation but you pay for reserved capacity. we can configure autoscaling with fenced limits so you get bursts within the reserved pool and fallback to hosted/shared pool only when the reserved is exhausted.
02:24 Sara: fallback worries me - if fallback sends requests to a quantized variant, what's the quality delta?
02:30 Marco: good question. our Optimize team has per-model quant profiles. typical INT8 for many transformer encoder-decoder variants yields small BLEU/ROUGE degradation for generation but sometimes hallucination risk rises on complex long-context prompts. we can gate fallback by strict regtests on your prompt set - we ran your sample prompts through INT8 and saw 1.8% drop in answer recall on the longest sequences.
02:52 Priya: hmm 1.8% might be ok if we document it in the SLA, but we need pre-approval from product on any quality regression.
03:00 Ava: that is a normal enterprise ask. we usually run canary and A/B on a representative subset. the rollout policy supports automatic rollback if quality drops past threshold.
03:12 Ethan: tell me more about KV prefetch and pinning — how does that help tail latency for 900-1500 token sequences?
03:19 Marco: KV cache helps reduce per-token compute for autoregressive decoding by storing past key/value for the attention layers. for long-context like yours, hits to the KV cache drastically cut compute on repeated prefixes. prefetch is predicting which KV pages you'll need and pinning them in GPU memory ahead of the decode. tradeoff: prefetching increases memory pressure; if you over-pin you reduce #concurrent sessions per GPU.
03:42 Sara: we have a lot of repeated prefixes in our EHR templates, so hit-rates could be high. can Redwood pin per-tenant KV in dedicated pools?
03:50 Marco: yes, in dedicated pools we can reserve a KV slab per tenant and tune eviction windows. in hosted multi-tenant we use adaptive eviction and soft pinning prioritized by recentness and weight. pinning in dedicated is more deterministic.
04:04 Priya: eviction behavior is critical. do you export eviction logs and hit/miss rates? we need to map that back to SLOs.
04:11 Marco: yes we ship detailed telemetry per-tenant: kv_hit_rate, kv_evictions, per-request decode tokens, and latency percentiles. I'll attach the sample eviction logs from our test run in the benchmark sheet.
04:24 Ethan: network questions - if we go VPC peering to Redwood hosted control plane with private deployment, what's expected egress and cross-region behavior? we need to avoid hops that add 50-100ms.
04:34 Ava: for our Private deployment we can do VPC peering in-region which keeps latency low. if you choose hosted but with VPC peering, the data path for inference stays in-region. for on-prem we ship an appliance, but that adds ops overhead.
04:47 Priya: security: KMS integration, SSO, audit logs. is there HSM option?
04:52 Marco: yes, we support customer-managed KMS (Cloud KMS/HSM) for key wrapping, SAML SSO, RBAC, and forwardable audit logs. HSM-backed KMS is supported for Private deployments. we'll include the SOC2/ISO artifacts.
05:06 Sara: ok back to batching — what's Redwood's default batching window and how do we tune for latency-sensitive small requests?
05:12 Marco: our runtime uses adaptive batching: it builds micro-batches up to a time window (default 6-12 ms) and up to a max batch size. for latency-sensitive workloads you can set strict max-latency windows (2-4 ms) and lower burst batch sizes. that increases per-token cost but improves p50/p95.
05:29 Ethan: can batching be tenant-aware so one tenant's batch doesn't get delayed waiting for other tenant's slow large sequences?
05:35 Marco: yes, we do tenant-priority batching. small requests from high-priority tenants are flushed earlier. in dedicated pools it's trivially isolated. in multi-tenant we mix but prioritize per policy.
05:45 Priya: what about continuous batching + kv cache interplay? if you delay for bigger batches you might miss prefetch windows?
05:52 Marco: exactly. there's a sweet spot: for predictable prefixes, prefetching into GPU memory before batching completes helps. we tune prefetch offsets relative to expected token throughput. it's workload specific; that's why we'd like your seq histograms.
06:05 Sara: i'm worried about cold-starts on long-context prompts — how do you mitigate?
06:09 Marco: we keep warmed model shards for heavy tenants in dedicated pools and can pre-warm KV for scheduled high-traffic windows. for ad-hoc long sequences we use progressive decoding heuristics to start partial responses while background prefetch completes. it's not perfect but reduces perceived latencies.
06:25 Ethan: capacity planning — what's the recommended overprovision for dedicated pool to handle 99th with spiky load?
06:31 Marco: typical recommendation is 20-30% headroom above your expected steady throughput for latency SLOs, and a small burst buffer for rare spikes. for extreme bursty loads we pair reserved capacity with fast cross-pool fallback and circuit-breaker throttles to protect core SLOs.
06:45 Priya: ok let's talk pilot design — we want to simulate noisy neighbor and validate tail behavior for 48 hours. what do you need?
06:52 Marco: we'll need a representative request trace (timestamps, seq lengths, concurrency) and a list of critical prompts. we'll run a dedicated pool sim + hosted shared sim and provide comparative p50/p95/p99 and kv metrics.
07:05 Ava: I'll coordinate scheduling with Ethan. we'll also include our canary rollback policy in the run.
07:10 Priya: thanks. one last question — billing implications if we reserve dedicated GPUs but then fallback to hosted shared during peaks?
07:17 Ava: you'll be billed for reserved capacity as committed, and the overflow into hosted is billed as overage at a different rate. we can model expected spend once we have your traces.
07:27 Ethan: ok makes sense.
07:30 Marco: i will push the kv benchmarks and per-model int8 matrices to the shared drive and annotate the quality regressions observed on your prompt set.
07:37 Priya: great. thanks everyone.
07:40 Ava: recap of next steps: Marco sends benchmarks and eviction logs; Ava shares SOC2/KMS docs; Priya shares seq distributions; schedule pilot kick-off; action items on the doc.
07:52 Ethan: we'll target first week of Jan for pilot kickoff.
07:56 Sara: i'll assemble the prompt set and a small A/B harness.
08:00 Ava: perfect, thanks all. meeting end.

Notes: audio transcript had occasional word swaps (e.g., "kv page" -> "k v page", "Triton" -> "T r i t o n"). references to shared artifacts: KV benchmark spreadsheet, canary policy doc, SOC2 package.
